      Month by month

      Hive work, set to local bloom

      Monthly handout

      One page for a month: what's blooming with its pollen color, the hive jobs, the key dates and the spray watch. Hand it out at meetings, post it at the sign-in table, or put it on the screen.

      Using the handout
      1. Pick the month above; it starts on this month. Next month's handout is the one to bring to a meeting.
      2. Print handout makes a one-page, letter-size PDF and opens the phone's print screen. Pick a printer, or choose Save as PDF to keep a copy.
      3. Save or share handout saves the same PDF to your Downloads and opens the share sheet, so you can email it, text it or put it in Google Drive.
      4. Save handout to print makes a one-page, letter-size PDF. Open it and print it like any document; on a phone, open it and use the share button to print or send it.
      5. Print it now prints the same page straight from your browser. (Inside the Claude app's viewer, use Save handout to print instead.)
      6. Save handout as PowerPoint slide puts the same month on one widescreen slide for a meeting, with speaker notes that walk through each plant.
      7. What's on it: each plant in bloom that month with its pellet color (a ? where no color is on record), its bloom window and nectar and pollen value; the month's hive jobs; the key dates that fall in the month; and what's likely being sprayed nearby. There are lines at the bottom for notes.
      8. Early or late spring: the handout follows the Early, Normal or Late setting in The year at a glance.
      9. Your own records stay off it. The handout never includes your bloom log or your contacts, so it's safe to share.
      Save the months as PowerPoint slides

      One slide per month, laid out like the monthly handout: what's blooming with pollen colors, hive jobs, key dates and spray watch, with speaker notes. Opens in PowerPoint, Keynote or Google Slides.

      How these were set. The hive tasks follow the NC State Beekeepers Association calendar for central North Carolina, moved a week or two earlier. That's the gap NC State's own bloom dates show between the Piedmont and the coastal plain: red maple opens around January 20 here against February 1 in the Piedmont, and tulip poplar around April 17 against April 25. Treat every date as the middle of a range; your own yard, your own year and your own records beat any calendar.

          Save as PowerPoint

          Using the slide in a club presentation
          1. Slides for this month and next month is the quickest way to get ready for a meeting: one file with a slide for each month, named like pollen-landing-board-september-october.pptx.
          2. Slide of what's showing above makes slides of whatever the buttons above are set to: this week, this month, next month or the whole year. The whole year runs to four slides.
          3. Each plant gets a pellet in its load color, the color name and its bloom window, with the major flows marked. Plants with no recorded pellet color get the same pellet with a ? in the middle, so members know to watch for them and report back.
          4. Speaker notes on each slide carry every plant's scientific name, where it grows here and what it gives the bees, ready to talk from.
          5. Getting it to the meeting: the slides are saved to your Downloads and the share sheet opens, so you can email them to yourself or put them in Google Drive, then open them on the computer you'll present from.
          6. Opening it: PowerPoint opens it directly. In Keynote, choose File, Open. In Google Slides, upload it to Google Drive and open it with Google Slides, or use File, Import slides in an existing deck to drop it into your presentation.
          7. Copying into your own deck: in PowerPoint, open both files, then copy the slide from the thumbnail list and paste it into your deck. Pick "Keep source formatting" to keep the colors.
          8. Colors on a projector are never exact. Say so, and have members match loads against what's in bloom rather than color alone.

          Read it as a clue, not a verdict. Watch the entrance for a few minutes around midmorning and match the loads going in against what's in bloom. Colors shift with light, moisture and how the bee packed the load, and no screen shows them exactly, so a rough match plus the bloom date is usually enough to tell what they're working. Colors are approximate, from the NC State Beekeepers Association's flowering-plants table and Wikipedia's list of pollen sources. Oak and corn colors are the European and general figures for those plants; ragweed's is one beekeeper's field report. Redbud, jessamine, huckleberry, tupelo, titi, crape myrtle, soybean, partridge pea, Spanish needles and thorny olive aren't recorded in any source we could find, so they show a pellet with a question mark. If your club members note what they see on the landing board, those gaps fill in fast.

          Bloom dates for red maple, blackberry, dandelion, huckleberry, sumac, tulip poplar, tupelo, holly, black gum, gallberry, sourwood, sweet pepperbush, goldenrod and aster are NC State University's coastal plain averages (Insect Note 1.04, Honey Plants of North Carolina). Hive tasks are adapted from the NCSBA calendar for central NC. Pollen colors come from the NCSBA flowering-plants table and Wikipedia's list of pollen sources, and are approximate; ragweed's is from a beekeeper's field report. Titi's purple-brood warning is from the NC Extension Plant Toolbox; cotton nectar notes from the NC Department of Agriculture. Other windows are typical for the area and marked as such.

          How backups work
          1. Exporting: tap Export backup file. The file is saved to your Downloads (open the Files app, sometimes called My Files, to see it) and the share sheet opens. Pick Gmail and send it to yourself, or Drive to put it in Google Drive, so it's safe if you lose the phone.
          2. Importing: tap Import a backup file and pick it from Downloads or Google Drive. The app tells you what it would add or replace and asks before changing anything.
          3. The spreadsheet opens in Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers, with how many days early or late each plant was against the local average. You can fix a date or add a row (keep the column headings, dates like 2026-04-12 or 4/12/2026) and import it back. A club can put several members' spreadsheets side by side.
          4. Moving to a new phone: export a backup on the old phone, install the app on the new one, then import the backup there.
          5. How often: the app reminds you after every few new dates. The newest backup is the only one you need; backup files have the date in their name.

          Your records in this app

          Read this before you uninstall or change phones

          The app keeps your bloom log, spray contacts, reminder choices and settings in the app itself, on this phone. Nothing is stored online. Clearing your web browser doesn't touch them, and installing an update to the app keeps them.

          Lost if
          • You uninstall the app, or clear its storage in the phone's Settings. This is the one to watch.
          • The phone is lost, stolen, broken or reset.
          • You switch to a new phone. Your records don't move over on their own.
          Safe no matter what
          • A backup file you've exported and kept off the phone, in your email or Google Drive. Import a backup file puts everything back.
          • Reminders you've added to Google Calendar. They live in your Google account, not here.
          • The calendar itself: bloom dates, pollen colors and hive jobs.

          The simple habit: after every few dates you log, export a backup file and send it to your email or Google Drive. The app reminds you when it's time. If anything is ever lost, install the app and use Import a backup file. (Android's own Google backup may also bring the app's records back on a new phone, but don't count on it.)

          Your browser and your records

          Read this before you clear your browser

          This page saves a few things inside the browser or app you open it in, on that one device. Nothing is stored online, so if the browser erases its saved site data, those things are gone for good unless you've kept a copy.

          Erased when site data is cleared
          • Your bloom log, every first-seen date for every year. This is the one that matters.
          • Your spray contacts.
          • Your reminder choices on this page (time, key dates, how you hear).
          • Your settings: early or late spring, filters, sort order and pollen view.
          Safe no matter what
          • Reminders you've already added to your phone, Google, Outlook or Yahoo calendar. They live in your calendar, not here.
          • A backup file you've kept somewhere safe, or a log you've emailed to yourself. Import a backup file or Get my log back puts everything back.
          • The calendar itself: bloom dates, pollen colors and hive jobs.
          What wipes it
          • Clearing "cookies and site data" (Chrome, Edge, Android, Firefox) or "Clear History and Website Data" (iPhone and iPad Safari). Clearing only "cached images and files" usually leaves your log alone.
          • Private or incognito windows. Everything is forgotten when the window closes, so don't keep your log in one.
          • iPhone and iPad Safari on its own: if you don't open the page for about a week, Safari can delete what it saved.
          • A new phone, a different browser, or reinstalling the browser or app. Each browser on each device keeps its own separate log; dates on your phone don't show up on your computer.
          • Cleaner and "speed booster" apps, and some browser settings that clear data every time the browser closes.
          How to clear your browser without losing your log

          Showing steps for

          • Chrome or Edge (computer or Android): in Clear browsing data, tick only Cached images and files and leave Cookies and other site data unticked.
          • iPhone or iPad Safari: avoid Clear History and Website Data. To tidy up other sites, go to Settings, Safari, Advanced, Website Data, and delete sites one at a time.
          • Firefox: in Clear recent history, tick Cache and leave Cookies and site data unticked.
          • Any browser: save a backup file or email your log to yourself first. Then it doesn't matter what gets cleared.

          The simple habit: after every few dates you log, back up on the My Log tab: email your log to yourself or save a backup file. The page reminds you when it's time. If anything is ever lost, use Import a backup file or Get my log back. On Android, the Android app keeps your log in the app itself, so clearing the browser can't touch it.

          Spraying and contacts

          Know who sprays near your bees, and who to call

          Most pesticide losses happen because nobody knew the bees were there. The fix is people knowing each other before the season starts.

          When spraying is likeliest around here

            Typical for the area's crops; your neighbors' schedules are what count, so ask them.

            Before the season
            • Map your yards on BeeCheck NC. It's free, and farmers, landscapers and spray crews can see where your hives are before they spray.
            • Register your apiaries with NCDA&CS. Under state rules, anyone hiring an aerial applicator to put out a bee-toxic pesticide must notify registered apiaries within a mile, 48 hours to 10 days ahead. There's a small fee.
            • Meet the grower next to each yard. Trade phone numbers, tell them where the hives sit, and ask for a call before they spray. Add them to your contacts below.
            • Ask your town or county about mosquito spraying: when they spray and how they give notice.
            • Put your name and number on each bee yard so anyone spraying nearby can reach you.
            When you hear spraying is coming
            • Ask what, when and where. Evening or night spraying, after the bees are in, is much safer; ask if they can do that.
            • Moving hives is the surest protection: screen the entrances at night when the foragers are home, strap the boxes, and move them out of the area.
            • Covering hives with wet burlap is a last resort. Never seal a hive; bees overheat and suffocate fast.
            If you suspect a bee kill
            • Piles of dead bees at the entrance, bees twitching or unable to fly, or foragers suddenly missing in good weather.
            • Take photos and video, and write down the date, time, weather, what's blooming and anything you saw sprayed.
            • Keep a sample of the dead bees, and of the plants they were working, in a clean bag in the freezer until you've talked to the state.
            • Call the NCDA&CS Pesticide Section right away at 984-236-4575, or use their online report form.
